newsitem.title: UK: Boeing wants no forecast duel with Airbus.
newsitem.headline: Boeing wants no forecast duel with Airbus.

text.p: Boeing Co's project director for market requirements, John Griffiths, told an IATA conference on Tuesday that he was "not interested in duelling forecasts" with Airbus Industrie consortium over the potential market for a new generation of large "superjumbos".

He was responding to Airbus marketing development manager Daniel Sallier saying that "the U.S. manufacturer is deliberately trying to play down this market's potential in order to retain its 27-year monopoly " of the big jet market.
Sallier was commenting on forecasts by Griffiths that the market through the year 2015 for aircraft of up to 600 passengers would be for 480 units versus earlier Airbus estimates of 1,380.

Sallier later told Reuters this was part of a Boeing attempt to inhibit the airlines and their financiers from committing to an original programme jumbo design such as Airbus' A3XX and continue relying on Boeing 747 derivatives.
Boeing has previously forecast that it would cost $5 billion to develop a stretch version of its 747, while Airbus has put a $8 billion price tax on its A3XX project.

Sallier added: "This is because Boeing, after its huge investment in the 777 programme and its two latest versions -- the 777-200 and 777-300 -- hasn't got the money to embark on a totally new design concept such as that envisaged by the European consortium," he said.
Boeing's Griffiths said markets like Japan to Hawaii and Japan to the U.S. West Coast as well as those overflying Japan from Asia to the West Coast are "begging for large-capacity jets".
But on other routes like the north Atlantic even existing 747s had a declining presence.
"This will not be an aircraft for the faint hearted," added Griffiths, "because there are already many existing aircraft which can perform the long-range mission."

And intercontinental traffic flows for which large jets are suited will be confined to fewer than 100 routes between key cities by 2015, with smaller Boeing 767 and other longhaul aircraft also competing on these same routes.
Griffiths said Boeing had identified 20 potential customers for large jets worldwide by 2015 with 10 in Asia, five in Europe and two in the U.S. and three in other markets.

"There is certainly a market," he added. "But the question is whether it is big enough to allow the manufacturers to make money and it is the way in which deregulation drives demand that will determine the answer to this question."
The Airbus consortium includes France's Aerospatiale, British Aerospace Plc, Germany's. Daimler-Benz Aerospace and Casa of Spain. -- Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax+44 171 542 5017
